kept.a:
Thanksgiving turkey, two ways on one plate: the Roasted Buttermilk-Brined Turkey Breast is one of the six entrées on the Thanksgiving Day menu, three courses for $80, served on Thanksgiving Day only.

The breast is brined in buttermilk and roasted. Salt in a brine seasons the meat right through and helps the lean white meat hold its juice in the oven, and buttermilk brings a gentle tang with the salt. The leg is braised, cooked slowly in liquid, which suits dark meat: it turns rich and tender. So the guest gets white meat and dark meat together.

Cornbread dressing is the Southern side of the holiday. Dressing is the same kind of mixture as stuffing, bread with herbs and broth, but baked in its own pan rather than inside the bird, and in the South it is made with cornbread. The jus is cranberry and rosemary: a jus is a light sauce from the meat’s own juices, here sharpened with tart fruit and the pine of rosemary.

How long the brine runs and what goes into the dressing are questions for the kitchen at lineup.

Lead with the holiday: this is the Thanksgiving turkey, and it comes two ways, so white meat and dark meat lovers are both happy. Offer it to the traditional guest and to the table ordering a family dinner. Say: “It’s our Thanksgiving turkey, a buttermilk-brined roast breast and a braised leg, with cornbread dressing and a cranberry jus.” Then offer a glass of red Burgundy: light Pinot Noir is a classic red with turkey and cranberry.

Asked: Is it white meat or dark meat?

Answer: Both. The breast is roasted white meat, brined in buttermilk, and the leg is braised, so there is dark meat on the plate too.

Asked: Is the dressing the same as stuffing?

Answer: The same idea, bread with herbs and broth, but baked in its own pan rather than inside the bird. In the South it is made with cornbread. What else is in ours is the kitchen’s to say.

Asked: Will it taste of buttermilk?

Answer: Not much. The brine seasons the meat and keeps it juicy, and at most it leaves a gentle tang.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only. Do not promise gravy: the menu lists a cranberry and rosemary jus, a light sauce, so if a guest asks for gravy, ask the kitchen. Learn at lineup what is in the cornbread dressing before you describe it, since Southern dressings often carry sausage, oysters or pecans, and never guess. A question about dairy or any diet goes to the kitchen. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a:
A hearty fall plate with a Louisiana glaze: the Bacon-Wrapped Pork Tenderloin is one of the six entrées on the Thanksgiving Day menu, three courses for $80, served on Thanksgiving Day only.

Pork tenderloin is a very lean, very tender cut with a mild flavor. That is why it is so often wrapped in bacon: the bacon protects the lean meat as it roasts, its fat bastes it, and it adds smoke and salt. The glaze is Louisiana cane syrup, sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles with nothing taken out, so it is sweeter and milder than molasses, with a buttery caramel taste.

The sides bring Italy and the American South together. Polenta is the cornmeal porridge of northern Italy, ground finer than grits. Mustard greens are the leaves of the mustard plant, peppery when raw and mellower and sweeter when cooked, a staple of Southern cooking. Roasted apples bring the fall fruit and a tart lift against the sweet glaze.

How the pork is cooked and sliced, and how the greens are cooked, are for the kitchen to tell you at lineup.

Offer it to the guest who wants a holiday plate but not the turkey, and to the guest who loves sweet and savory together. Say: “It’s pork tenderloin wrapped in bacon with a Louisiana cane syrup glaze, on polenta with mustard greens and roasted apples.” Name the cane syrup: it is local, and guests like hearing where a flavor comes from. Then offer the Mosel Riesling by the glass, whose touch of sweetness meets the glaze and the apples while its acidity cuts the bacon.

Asked: What is cane syrup?

Answer: Louisiana sugar cane juice boiled down until thick. It is sweeter and milder than molasses, with a caramel taste.

Asked: What is polenta?

Answer: The cornmeal porridge of northern Italy, a cousin of our grits, ground finer.

Asked: Can I have the pork cooked medium?

Answer: Ask the kitchen. How the tenderloin is cooked and to what temperature is the chef’s call, so check at lineup before you promise a temperature.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only. The glaze is sweet, so tell a guest who dislikes sweet sauces before they order. Do not promise a temperature for the pork until the kitchen tells you how it is cooked. The bacon is part of the dish, and the polenta and greens may carry butter or pork, so any question about a diet goes to the kitchen. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a:
The steak dinner of the holiday menu: the Herb Roasted Beef Tenderloin is one of the six entrées on the Thanksgiving Day menu, three courses for $80, served on Thanksgiving Day only.

Tenderloin is the cut that gives filet mignon: lean, fine grained and very tender. Here it is roasted with herbs. The sauce is au poivre, French for with pepper, the sauce of steak au poivre, a classic of the French bistro. In the classic, coarsely crushed peppercorns meet a pan sauce of shallots, Cognac and cream, and tenderloin is the usual cut for it. How our kitchen makes its sauce is for lineup.

Pommes purée is the French style of mashed potatoes: the potatoes are riced, often passed through a fine sieve, and worked with a great deal of butter until silky. Brussels sprouts take their name from the region of Brussels in Belgium, where they were a popular crop by the sixteenth century; roasting browns their edges and makes them nutty and sweet.

It is a rich plate built for a red wine.

Offer it to the guest who wants red meat on the holiday and to the steakhouse regular. Lead with the sauce, since au poivre is a classic guests recognize. Say: “It’s herb roasted beef tenderloin with a French peppercorn sauce, silky pommes purée and roasted Brussels sprouts.” Take the temperature with the order, as the kitchen asks, and offer the Bordeaux by the glass, whose cassis and cedar stand up to the pepper.

Asked: What is au poivre?

Answer: French for with pepper. It is a peppercorn sauce, the one on the bistro classic steak au poivre. How hot ours is, the kitchen can tell you.

Asked: Is this a filet?

Answer: It is beef tenderloin, the same cut filet mignon comes from, roasted with herbs.

Asked: What is pommes purée?

Answer: The French style of mashed potatoes: very smooth, with a lot of butter worked in.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only. Ask the kitchen at lineup how the tenderloin is roasted and what temperatures it can be cooked to before you take an order. The pepper sauce can be strong, so offer it on the side only if the kitchen says it can be done. The sauce and the potatoes are rich with butter and may carry cream, so a question about dairy or any diet goes to the kitchen. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a:
A taste of Cajun country on the holiday menu: the Shrimp Sauce Piquante is one of the six entrées on the Thanksgiving Day menu, three courses for $80, served on Thanksgiving Day only.

Sauce piquante, piquant meaning sharp or spicy, is a Louisiana dish more than a sauce: a hot, tomato based stew, usually started on a roux with the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper, that smothers whatever the cook has, chicken, catfish, turtle, rabbit, alligator or shrimp, and is served over rice. It has long been popular in Acadiana.

Ours is shrimp in a Creole tomato gravy. The rice is a pilaf of popcorn rice, the Louisiana aromatic long grain that smells of popcorn as it cooks; in a pilaf the grains are cooked in fat before the liquid goes in, so they stay separate. Pickled peppers bring a sharp, bright bite against the warm tomato.

How hot the kitchen makes it, which peppers are pickled and what goes into the gravy are questions for lineup.

Offer it to the guest who wants a Louisiana dish on the holiday, to the seafood lover and to anyone who asks for something with a little heat. Say: “It’s shrimp sauce piquante, a Cajun classic: shrimp in a peppery Creole tomato gravy over popcorn rice, with pickled peppers.” Tell the guest how hot it runs once the kitchen has told you, and offer the Provence rosé by the glass, which is fresh enough for tomato and gentle with spice.

Asked: How spicy is it?

Answer: Piquante means sharp or spicy, and the dish is traditionally hot. How hot ours is, the kitchen tells us at lineup, so ask before you promise.

Asked: What is popcorn rice?

Answer: A Louisiana aromatic long grain rice that really does smell of popcorn as it cooks. Here it is cooked as a pilaf, so the grains stay separate.

Asked: Is it like shrimp Creole?

Answer: A cousin. Both are shrimp in a tomato sauce over rice; sauce piquante is the spicier Cajun country version, usually built on a roux.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only. Learn at lineup how hot the kitchen makes it, and steer a guest who wants no heat to the redfish or the turkey. Do not call it gumbo or étouffée: it is its own dish. Shrimp, a roux and the gravy all raise questions, so any question about shellfish, flour or a diet goes to the kitchen. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a:
A New Orleans classic style on a Gulf fish: the Redfish Meunière is one of the six entrées on the Thanksgiving Day menu, three courses for $80, served on Thanksgiving Day only.

À la meunière means in the style of the miller’s wife. The usual reason given is the flour: in the classic, the fish is dredged in flour, cooked in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley. In New Orleans the style is a bedrock of Creole cooking, best known as trout meunière, and it suits the mild, firm fish of the Gulf.

Ours is redfish, the red drum, with brown butter, lemon and capers. Brown butter is butter cooked until its milk solids toast and smell of hazelnut; lemon sharpens it and capers add a briny pop.

Under the fish is an écrasé, French for crushed: potatoes and leeks crushed with a fork or masher rather than puréed smooth, so they keep some texture. Whether the kitchen flours the fish, and where the redfish comes from, are questions for lineup.

Offer it to the fish lover, to the guest who wants something lighter than the meats and to anyone who knows trout meunière. Say: “It’s redfish meunière, a New Orleans classic: brown butter, lemon and capers over crushed potatoes and leeks.” Give the word for the potatoes, écrasé, because guests enjoy learning it, then offer the Chardonnay by the glass, whose creamy texture and bright acidity sit right with brown butter and lemon.

Asked: What does meunière mean?

Answer: In the style of the miller’s wife. In the classic, the fish is dusted in flour and cooked in butter, then finished with brown butter and lemon.

Asked: What kind of fish is redfish?

Answer: Red drum, a Gulf fish with mild, firm, slightly sweet white flesh. Where ours comes from, the kitchen can tell you.

Asked: What is an écrasé?

Answer: French for crushed: potatoes and leeks crushed rather than mashed smooth, so they keep a little texture.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only. The word redfish also brings up the past Redfish Véronique in the app: this is a different dish, so do not mix them up. Do not promise the fish is floured or say where it comes from until the kitchen tells you. Fish, butter and a possible flour dusting all raise questions, so any question about fish, dairy, flour or a diet goes to the kitchen. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a:
Grillades and grits, the old Creole breakfast, comes to the holiday dinner as the Veal Grillades, one of the six entrées on the Thanksgiving Day menu, three courses for $80, served on Thanksgiving Day only.

Grillades are thin slices of veal or beef, pounded and braised in gravy until tender, and served over grits. The word comes from the French for to grill, but they are not grilled. The grillades in the cookbooks of the late 1800s were veal medallions simmered in gravy; a recipe ran in The Daily Picayune in 1898, and a breakfast menu in the Times-Democrat listed grillades and grits in 1900. Carnival kings and queens still serve them at krewe breakfasts after their balls.

Ours adds debris, the tender shreds of roast that fall into the gravy, best known on the roast beef po’boy, and piperade, a Basque and Gascon dish of peppers, onion and tomato. The cheddar grits and a poached egg make it rich: the yolk becomes part of the sauce. Which roast gives the debris is a question for lineup.

Offer it to the guest who wants a true New Orleans dish, to the local who grew up on grillades at brunch and to the guest who loves comfort food. Say: “It’s veal grillades, the Creole brunch classic, over cheddar grits with debris, piperade and a poached egg.” Tell the story in one line, Carnival krewes still serve grillades after their balls, then offer the Barbera by the glass, bright enough for the gravy and the cheese.

Asked: What are grillades?

Answer: Thin slices of veal, pounded and simmered in gravy until tender, a Creole breakfast classic usually served over grits. Despite the name they are not grilled.

Asked: What is debris?

Answer: The tender shreds of roast that fall into the gravy as it cooks, the same debris as on a roast beef po’boy. Which roast ours comes from, the kitchen can tell you.

Asked: What is piperade?

Answer: A Basque dish of sweet peppers, onion and tomato cooked down together.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only. Do not call the veal grilled: grillades are simmered in gravy. The debris may come from a different meat than the veal, so learn at lineup what it is before you describe it. The egg is poached and the yolk runs, so tell the guest who wants it firm to ask. Cheese, egg and gravy all raise questions, so any question about dairy, eggs or a diet goes to the kitchen. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.
